content: Chronic cough, defined as a cough lasting longer than four weeks, is a prevalent issue worldwide. It imposes significant economic burdens and causes distress to both children and their parents. Neglecting chronic cough can result in delayed diagnosis and progression of serious underlying respiratory conditions. Clinical guidelines have been shown to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of patient care, aiding in clinical decision-making. Specific guidelines for managing chronic cough have been developed, but treatment recommendations vary widely. This variability underscores the importance of tailored clinical pathways for children, as the causes and treatments for chronic cough in children differ significantly from those in adults. A systematic evaluation of evidence-based clinical pathways for managing chronic cough in children could improve clinical practice and patient outcomes. Management algorithms, such as those provided by the American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) and the British Thoracic Society (BTS), have the potential to enhance clinical outcomes. The objective of this study was to assess the effectiveness of using a clinical pathway in managing chronic cough in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, as well as review articles and reference lists of relevant studies. The most recent search was completed in January 2014. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a parallel-group design that compared the use of a clinical pathway versus no clinical pathway for treating chronic cough in children under 18 years of age. Two independent reviewers screened studies for inclusion and performed data extraction. Only one study met the inclusion criteria. This multi-center trial was conducted across five Australian hospitals and included 272 children with chronic cough. Participants were randomly assigned to either an early referral group (two weeks) or a delayed referral group (six weeks) for evaluation by respiratory specialists who utilized a cough management pathway. The primary outcome was clinical failure at six weeks post-randomization, defined as less than 75% improvement in cough score or total resolution of cough for fewer than three consecutive days. The results demonstrated that clinical failure was significantly lower in the early referral group compared to the delayed referral group. The odds ratio (OR) for clinical failure was 0.35 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.21 to 0.58), indicating that one additional child would benefit for every five children treated using the clinical pathway (number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome [NNTB] = 5, 95% CI 3 to 9). Parent-reported quality of life scores specific to cough were significantly better in the early referral group, with a mean difference (MD) of 0.60 (95% CI 0.19 to 1.01). Additionally, the duration of cough post-randomization was significantly shorter in the early referral group compared to the delayed referral group, with a mean difference of -2.70 weeks (95% CI -4.26 to -1.14). In conclusion, current evidence suggests that implementing a clinical algorithm for managing chronic cough in children within hospital outpatient settings is more effective than wait-list care. However, further high-quality randomized controlled trials are necessary to evaluate the effectiveness of cough management pathways in primary care and general practitioner settings.
